chapter_title: Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents
learning_objective: The learner will identify the five layers of the Theodosian land walls in the order an attacker from the west meets them, with no more than one placement error.
specification:
Type: infographic **sim-id:** theodosian-walls-layers
**Library:** html
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Remember
**Bloom Verb:** identify
**Learning Objective:** The learner will identify the five layers of the Theodosian land walls in the order an attacker from the west meets them, with no more than one placement error. **Prerequisites:** moat, terrace, tower, breach, outer wall, inner wall, peribolos (all defined in the section "The Theodosian Walls" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** Part 1: the learner places five unlabeled layer names into five positions on the cross-section, from outside (west) to inside (east), and submits. A position is correct when it matches the Order column in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 positions correct on the first submission. Part 2: three multiple-choice questions, each correct when it matches the Answer column. Clicking callouts after submission is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) The walls were one thick wall. (2) The moat was the strongest defense. (3) The outer wall was taller than the inner wall. (4) The walls were named for Theodosius I. (5) The walls were never breached before 1453 (the crusaders broke in from the harbor in 1204, not through the land walls). **Instructional Rationale:** At the Remember level, the learner must be able to retrieve the layers and their order without support. Placing the names on a cross-section before the callouts are revealed is that retrieval; the three questions that follow check the reason for the order. **Content:** A schematic cross-section of the land walls, west (outside, toward Thrace) on one side and east (inside, the city) on the other. Each layer is drawn with relative heights correct (inner wall taller than outer wall, moat below ground level). The drawing is labeled "Schematic; not to scale." | Order (outside to inside) | Layer | Approximate size | Callout text (revealed after submission) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Moat | About 20 m wide, several meters deep, with a low battlemented wall on its inner edge | Kept siege towers, rams and miners at a distance. | | 2 | Outer terrace | A narrow strip between the moat and the outer wall | Open ground where attackers were exposed to fire from both walls. | | 3 | Outer wall | About 8.5 m high and 2 m thick, with smaller towers of its own | The first wall an attacker had to climb or break. | | 4 | Inner terrace (peribolos) | About 15 to 20 m wide | Where defenders gathered; any attacker who crossed the outer wall was trapped here under fire from above. | | 5 | Inner wall | About 12 m high and nearly 5 m thick, with 96 towers up to about 20 m tall | The main wall. Its towers were set to cover the gaps between the outer towers. | Total depth from moat edge to inner wall: about 60 m. Length of the land walls: about 5.7 km. Completed in 413 under Theodosius II; rebuilt in less than two months after the earthquake of 447. Questions in Part 2: | # | Question | Choices | Answer | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Why is the inner wall taller than the outer wall? | So defenders on it could shoot over the outer wall at attackers; So it could be seen from the sea; Because it was built later; It is not taller | So defenders on it could shoot over the outer wall at attackers | Two heights let defenders fire from two levels at once. | | 2 | Which emperor completed the land walls in 413? | Constantine I; Theodosius I; Theodosius II; Justinian | Theodosius II | Theodosius I died in 395; his grandson Theodosius II completed the walls in 413. | | 3 | How did the crusaders get into the city in 1204? | Through a breach in the land walls; From the Golden Horn, over the sea walls; Through a tunnel; The gates were opened by treaty | From the Golden Horn, over the sea walls | The land walls held; the attack came from the harbor, where the sea walls were lower. | **Provenance:** All dimensions and dates are from this chapter's section "The Theodosian Walls," which uses commonly cited approximate figures; the sim must label the dimensions "approximate." **Rules:** Part 1 is scored per position: 5 positions, one point each. A layer name may be placed in only one position. Submission is allowed only when all five positions are filled. Part 2 is scored per question, one attempt each. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees the cross-section with five empty positions and five layer names in random order. 2. The learner places each name in a position, can rearrange freely, and submits. 3. Each position is marked correct or incorrect, the correct names are shown, and all five callouts become available. 4. The learner opens any callout to read its size and purpose. 5. The learner answers the three questions in Part 2, one at a time. 6. The learner should notice that the defense depended on depth and height working together, not on any single wall. **Feedback:** Part 1: one submission. Correct position: "Correct: ." Incorrect: "This position is the ." After submission: "n of 5 layers placed correctly." Part 2: three questions in fixed order, one attempt each; correct "Right." plus the Why text; incorrect "Not quite." plus the Why text, with the answer revealed. Final score: "Layers n of 5, questions m of 3." A Restart button clears both parts and reshuffles the layer names. **Starting State:** The empty cross-section with "West: Thrace" on the outside and "East: the city" on the inside, five layer names to place, and the question "An army arrives from the west. What does it meet first, and what last?" **Chapter Anchors:** Five layers: moat, outer terrace, outer wall, inner terrace (peribolos), inner wall. Moat about 20 m wide; outer wall about 8.5 m high, 2 m thick, with smaller towers; inner terrace 15 to 20 m wide; inner wall about 12 m high, nearly 5 m thick, 96 towers up to about 20 m tall; total depth about 60 m; length about 5.7 km; completed 413; earthquake January 447, rebuilt in less than two months.
